source.title: The behavioural final common path
source.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B

confidence_rationale: Foundational ethological formalisation of drive arbitration: motivational candidates compete for a single behavioural final common path because an animal cannot do more than one thing at a time, with the winner set by 'degree of competitiveness' in a causal-factor space. This is the conceptual ancestor of MECH-394's per-candidate competition and supplies the 'candidate'/'competitiveness' vocabulary REE's E3 scoring uses. Held at 0.66 because its core mutual-exclusivity axiom (behavioural classes cannot co-occur) is the winner-take-all pole that tensions with MECH-394's explicit 'soft-competitive ... not a single-axis winner' commitment, and the empirical content is 1975 dove hunger/thirst measurement.
failure_signatures: The framework axiomatises that behavioural classes are mutually exclusive (the animal does exactly one thing), giving a winner-take-all final common path. MECH-394 explicitly rejects a single-axis winner in favour of soft competition, so McFarland & Sibly anchor the WTA pole the REE policy must decide AGAINST -- it supports competition-among-candidates but not the soft-blend specifically.

Causal-factor-space isoclines are a descriptive measurement framework fitted to dove hunger/thirst; it does not specify the neural mechanism of competition, so it constrains the functional form of arbitration but is silent on implementation.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Any model of the reversible motivational processes governing behaviour can be represented by isoclines in a multidimensional causal-factor space, given that behavioural classes are mutually exclusive (cannot occur simultaneously) and incompatible actions are uniquely determined by a set of causal factors. Isoclines join points of equal 'degree of competitiveness' of a particular 'candidate' for overt expression; competition between candidates is the inevitable consequence of the animal being unable to do more than one thing at a time, and occurs in the behavioural final common path. Demonstrated by measuring hunger and thirst in doves.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-394 asserts that simultaneously-active drives are arbitrated by soft-competitive orchestration producing one behavioural output. McFarland & Sibly are the foundational statement of exactly this picture: drives are causal factors, behavioural options are 'candidates', and arbitration is the competition for a single behavioural final common path scored by each candidate's 'degree of competitiveness'. REE's E3 already scores per-candidate competitiveness (score_bias contributions, MECH-295), so this paper is arguably the conceptual ancestor of REE's arbitration vocabulary -- the multidrive policy MECH-394 wants is the modern, soft-competitive generalisation of the behavioural final common path. It frames the central V4 design fork: McFarland & Sibly's strict mutual-exclusivity is the WTA endpoint; MECH-394 chooses a softer competition between those poles.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The framework's mutual-exclusivity axiom (one behaviour at a time) is a winner-take-all commitment that MECH-394 deliberately relaxes; so this evidences the candidate-competition SKELETON of MECH-394, not its soft-competitive specifics, and it actively marks the WTA pole the policy must argue against. It is a 1975 behavioural/descriptive framework (dove hunger/thirst), silent on neural mechanism; transfer to a computational drive register assumes the causal-factor-space abstraction is substrate-general.
mapping.source_context: Theoretical ethology with behavioural measurement: causal-factor-space formalism applied to the quantification of hunger and thirst competition in doves.

confidence_components.notes: Foundational, canonical ethology (Phil Trans R Soc). Mapping_fidelity is the highest in this set on conceptual grounds -- 'candidate'/'competitiveness'/'final common path' is almost REE's own E3 language -- but transfer_risk is elevated by the 1975 vintage, the dove-behavioural empirical base, and the WTA-vs-soft-blend divergence.
